title: Bach: Brandenburg Concerto No. 5, third movement

tips.title: Concertino, ripieno, continuo
tips.body: The **concertino** is the small group of soloists, here flute, violin and harpsichord. The **ripieno** is the larger accompanying group. The **continuo** is the bass line plus a chordal instrument. Know which instrument sits where.

tips.title: Fugal style is not a fugue
tips.body: The movement **begins in fugal style**, with entries imitating each other, but it is not a fugue as a whole. Saying "it is a fugue" overstates it; saying "it begins fugally" is precise.

tips.title: Explain the harpsichord's unusual role
tips.body: Normally a continuo instrument keeping the harmony going, here it is promoted to a **soloist** with an extended solo passage. That promotion is what makes the movement famous, and it is worth saying.

tips.title: Name the group before the instrument
tips.body: Say whether a line belongs to the **concertino**, the **ripieno** or the **continuo** before naming the instrument playing it. Baroque concerto questions are about the interplay between those groups, and an answer built on the groups reads as analysis rather than a list.

steps.title: Where this set work sits
steps.body:
This is one of the two **instrumental music 1700 to 1820** set works; the other is Beethoven's *Pathétique* sonata, which you meet in Year 11. Section B can set this movement against an unfamiliar piece from the same area of study, so you compare by element.

Johann Sebastian Bach (1685 to 1750) is regarded as one of the greatest composers of the **Baroque** era. He worked mainly as a church organist, music director and composer in central Germany. When the Brandenburg Concertos were written he was **Kapellmeister**, court music director, at **Köthen from 1717 to 1723**.

That job matters. The castle grounds had a chapel, but **Prince Leopold** preferred not to have elaborate church music, so Bach's duties there were mainly **secular**, meaning non-religious. The prince was himself an enthusiastic amateur musician who encouraged Bach to write instrumental music. In six years Bach wrote most of his best-known instrumental works: these concertos, the six solo cello suites, the sonatas and partitas for solo violin, and the *Well-Tempered Clavier*.

steps.title: The facts to know cold
steps.body:
- The six Brandenburg Concertos were written between **1711 and 1720**, and in **1721** were dedicated to **Christian Ludwig, the Margrave of Brandenburg**.
- They were not called the *Brandenburg* Concertos until after their **rediscovery in the 19th century**.
- Almost certainly the music was never played by the Margrave's own musicians.
- Performances at Köthen were held in **rooms in the castle**, for a small number of dignitaries. There was a core of **eight or nine professional musicians**.
- So this is **chamber music**, not orchestral music in the modern sense. It is likely there was only **one player to a part**.
- Technically the piece is a **concerto grosso**: a concerto for a large number of instrumental parts.

steps.title: Concertino, ripieno and continuo
steps.body:
A concerto grosso has two groups, and the exam expects the words.

- The **concertino** is the solo group. Here it is **flute, violin and harpsichord**.
- The **ripieno** is the string orchestra. Bach breaks a rule here: it has **only one violin part**, where there would normally be two.
- The **continuo** is the Baroque bass-and-chords team: one or more bass instruments such as cello and double bass, plus at least one chordal instrument, usually the harpsichord.

The continuo player reads a **figured bass**: a shorthand of numbers written under the bass notes telling the player which chord to fill in with the right hand. That is called **realising** the harmony.

The flute here is a **Baroque flute**, made of wood with finger holes and just one metal key, so it is quieter than a modern flute. That quietness shapes the dynamics, as the next step shows.

steps.title: The harpsichord breaks the rules
steps.body:
This is the single most examinable thing about the concerto. Bach gives the harpsichord an **extended virtuoso solo part**, and this concerto is regarded as the **first concerto for keyboard solo in musical history**.

What makes it difficult:

- **rapid scalic runs** in both the right and the left hand
- passages where **both hands play trills at the same time**
- the first movement even has an extended **cadenza**, an unaccompanied solo section

Bach probably played the part himself. Only occasionally does the harpsichord drop back into playing **continuo chords**, for example at bars 29 to 37, and it is in those passages that a figured bass appears.

The mechanical action of a harpsichord means it **cannot change dynamics** by touch, unless a two-manual instrument is available, and the evidence suggests a single manual was used here. So there are **no dynamic markings for the harpsichord** in the original score.

steps.title: Dynamics, and why there are so few
steps.body:
Baroque scores carry far fewer markings than later music, and here there is a practical reason as well as a stylistic one.

The harpsichord cannot vary its volume by touch, so it has **no dynamic markings at all**. On the few occasions where any instrument does have one, it is there largely for **balance**, to make sure a particular line can be heard.

The clearest example: the **solo violin is marked *piano* at the beginning of the middle section**, so that it does not drown the tune, which is on the quieter solo flute. That is a question waiting to be asked, and the answer is balance, not expression.

steps.title: Structure: a large ternary shape
steps.body:
Most Baroque concerto movements use **ritornello** form, as Vivaldi's do: a returning orchestral idea alternating with solo episodes. This movement is different. It is a large **ternary** structure, **ABA**.

The table gives the sections with their bar numbers. Three details earn marks:

- the middle section's **new flute theme has many similarities to the main one**, so it does not sound like a different piece
- **fragments of the A theme keep appearing inside B**, which is a technique Bach used often, and it is why the return never feels entirely conclusive
- the final A begins with an **extra D major chord in the continuo**, put there to re-establish the tonic

steps.title: Texture: fugal, but not a fugue
steps.body:
The texture is **polyphonic**, also called **contrapuntal**: several independent melodic strands sounding together.

The movement **begins in fugal style**. A fugue is a piece that uses imitation almost throughout. This is **not an actual fugue**, but it uses fugal characteristics, and the opening four bars are the example to quote. Watch the order of entries:

1. the **subject**, the main theme, in the **solo violin**
2. the **answer** in the **flute**, two bars later, giving **two-part imitation**
3. four more bars, then the **harpsichord left hand** enters with the subject
4. two bars after that the **right hand** answers, so the harpsichord is in two-part counterpoint
5. once both hands are playing, the music is in **four-part counterpoint**

Elsewhere the flute and violin sometimes play **in thirds**, and the harpsichord does too. When the ripieno is playing, flute and violin sometimes **double each other in unison**, for example at bar 33. The bass line under the new middle-section theme has a **tonic pedal on B**.

the answer, two bars later: four-part counterpoint once both hands play

steps.title: Melody, harmony and the gigue rhythm
steps.body:
**Melody.** Much of the music is **conjunct**, moving by step, as at bar 2, though there are leaps, such as the fourths in bar 1. The conjunct writing is often extended into **scalic runs**, especially in the harpsichord. There is a **rising sequence at bar 137**, a short phrase repeated a step higher each time. Ornaments are occasional: **trills** in the harpsichord at bar 19, and **appoggiaturas** in the middle-section theme when it returns in A major at bar 148.

**Tonality.** D major, diatonic. The B section modulates to the **dominant, A major**, and the **relative minor, B minor**.

**Harmony.** Functional, using the standard chords of the time: mostly **I, IV and V**, with occasional **II and VI**, and **dominant sevenths in various inversions**. Chords are mainly **root position and first inversion**. **Perfect cadences** announce the ends of sections, and **suspensions** appear occasionally, such as the 9 to 8 suspension at bar 130.

**Metre and rhythm.** The metre is **2/4**, duple time, two beats to a bar, though the music could equally be written in **6/8** compound time. It is essentially a Baroque **gigue**, a dance in compound duple time. **Triplets and dotted rhythms** run throughout, and the dotted quaver and semiquaver of bar 1 would have been played in triplet rhythm: the dotted quaver taking two-thirds of a beat and the semiquaver one-third.

steps.title: Going deeper: answering a how question, and comparing
steps.body:
**Tie every device to an effect.** *The harpsichord plays runs* is a feature. *The harpsichord's rapid scalic runs in both hands turn the continuo instrument into the soloist, which is why this is called the first keyboard concerto* is an answer. Name the device, say what it does, and say where it happens.

**Comparing by element.** Section B sets this movement against an unfamiliar piece from the same area of study. Write melody in both, then texture in both, then harmony, then forces. Never a paragraph on each piece in turn.

**The comparison that pays here** is texture. Most later instrumental music is **homophonic**, a tune with accompaniment. This is **polyphonic**, several independent lines at once, opening in fugal style. If the unfamiliar piece is Classical, that difference alone can carry a paragraph, with the fugal entry order as your evidence.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **J S Bach**, 1685 to 1750, Baroque; Kapellmeister at **Köthen, 1717 to 1723**. Six concertos written **1711 to 1720**, dedicated **1721** to **Christian Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg**; named only after their 19th-century rediscovery.
- **Concerto grosso**, chamber music, likely one player to a part. **Concertino**: flute, violin, harpsichord. **Ripieno**: strings with only one violin part. **Continuo**: bass plus chords realised from a **figured bass**.
- The harpsichord has an extended **virtuoso** part: the **first concerto for keyboard solo**. Rapid scalic runs in both hands, simultaneous trills, a cadenza in the first movement.
- **No dynamics** for the harpsichord; the few markings are for **balance**, such as the violin's *piano* under the flute tune.
- **Large ternary, ABA**: A bars 1 to 78 in D major, B bars 79 to 232 from B minor, A from bar 233 after an extra D major continuo chord.
- **Polyphonic**, opening in fugal style: violin subject, flute answer, then harpsichord left hand and right hand, giving four-part counterpoint.
- **D major**, diatonic; functional harmony, perfect cadences, a 9 to 8 suspension at bar 130.
- **2/4**, but a **gigue** in effect: triplets and dotted rhythms throughout.

rows: D major; 2/4, felt as a compound-duple gigue

questions.modelAnswer: The texture is **polyphonic**, or contrapuntal: several independent melodic strands sound at once rather than a tune over chords. The movement **begins in fugal style**, and although it is not an actual fugue it uses fugal characteristics, with the opening four bars the clearest example. The **subject** is stated by the **solo violin** and **answered by the flute two bars later**, giving **two-part imitation**. After four further bars the **harpsichord's left hand** enters with the subject, and the **right hand answers two bars after that**, so the harpsichord is itself in two-part counterpoint; once both hands are sounding the music is in **four-part counterpoint**. The texture is not uniformly fugal: the flute and violin sometimes move **in thirds**, and when the ripieno is playing they sometimes **double each other in unison**, as at bar 33. Under the new theme of the middle section the bass holds a **tonic pedal on B**.

questions.prompt: This movement uses functional harmony. Which best describes it?
questions.solution: **Functional** harmony uses the standard chords of the time: predominantly **I, IV and V**, with occasional **II and VI**, and dominant sevenths in various inversions, mostly in root position and first inversion.

questions.prompt: A student writes: *this movement is in ritornello form, like all Baroque concertos.* Evaluate that statement.
questions.solution: The student is wrong about this movement. Ritornello form, in which a returning orchestral idea alternates with solo episodes, is the standard shape used by composers such as Vivaldi, so the generalisation is understandable. This movement is instead a large ternary structure, ABA: A in D major to bar 78, B from bar 79 beginning in B minor, and the opening section returning at bar 233. There is a grain of truth in the claim, because the return of A material has something of a ritornello about it and fragments of the A theme appear throughout B, so the sections are never entirely separate. But the movement is built on one large return, not on repeated alternation, so ternary is the better description.

questions.modelAnswer: The student is right about Baroque concertos in general and wrong about this one. **Ritornello form**, in which a returning orchestral idea alternates with solo episodes, is the standard shape, and Vivaldi's concertos use it, so the generalisation is understandable. This movement, though, is a **large ternary structure, ABA**: the A section runs from bar 1 to bar 78 in D major, the B section from bar 79 begins in the relative minor, B minor, and the opening section returns at bar 233, announced by an extra D major chord in the continuo. There is a grain of truth in the claim, because **fragments of the A theme appear frequently inside B**, so the return is never entirely conclusive and the movement does keep circling back to its opening material. But that is Bach weaving one idea through a ternary shape, not the repeated alternation of ritornello form, so **ternary is the better description**.

examTechnique.body:
Section A questions on this set work are short and precise: one term for one mark, spelled correctly. Know the facts cold — Bach, Baroque, Köthen, concerto grosso, concertino of flute, violin and harpsichord, D major, large ternary — so no time goes on recalling them.

For anything longer, tie the device to its effect and say where it happens. Bar numbers are the strongest evidence you can give: the fugal entries at the opening, the trills at bar 19, the continuo chords at bars 29 to 37, the suspension at bar 130, the rising sequence at bar 137, the appoggiaturas at bar 148, the return at bar 233.

Section B sets this against an unfamiliar piece from the same area of study. Compare **by element**, both pieces in every paragraph, and end with a judgement. Texture is usually the richest comparison, because this movement is polyphonic where most later instrumental music is homophonic.
examinerErrors: Calling the movement a fugue. It **begins in fugal style** but is not an actual fugue.
Saying it is in ritornello form because it is a Baroque concerto. This movement is large ternary, ABA.
Naming the concertino as two violins. Here it is flute, violin and harpsichord.
Treating the harpsichord as a continuo instrument only. Its extended virtuoso part is the whole point of the concerto.
Explaining the violin's *piano* marking as expression. It is there for **balance**, so the quieter Baroque flute can be heard.
Describing the texture as homophonic. Several independent lines sound together, so it is polyphonic.
Giving the B section's key as A major. It **begins** in B minor and ends with a perfect cadence in B minor, reaching A major on the way.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer names the form and contrasts it with the ritornello norm, gives the fugal entries in order with the two-bar spacing, and separates the harpsichord's two jobs, soloist and continuo, with bar numbers for each. It explains the dynamics as balance rather than expression, uses the correct terms (concertino, ripieno, continuo, figured bass, appoggiatura, suspension, gigue) without hesitating, and in Section B compares element by element with both pieces in every paragraph, ending on a judgement.
